units.title: Hello, JavaScript
units.summary: Write your first program, print text and numbers with console.log and learn what a statement is.

lesson.md: JavaScript is the language of the web. Every browser can run it, and with Node.js it also runs on your computer and on servers. A program is a list of instructions that the computer runs from top to bottom.
To show something on the screen, you use `console.log()`. Put the value you want to show between the parentheses.

lesson.code: console.log("Hello, world!");

lesson.md: Each instruction is a **statement**. You end a statement with a semicolon `;` and usually write one statement per line. The program runs the lines in order.

Text in quotes is a **string**. You can use double quotes `"Hi"` or single quotes `'Hi'`. Numbers have no quotes. JavaScript can calculate with them: `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies and `/` divides.

`console.log()` can show several values at once. Separate them with commas. It prints them on one line with a space between them. Note the difference: `"2 + 3"` is a string, so it is printed as it is.
A **comment** starts with `//`. JavaScript ignores everything after `//` until the end of the line. In this course, comments only show results, for example `// 5`.
JavaScript is **case-sensitive**. `console.log` works, but `Console.log` or `console.Log` stops the program with an error.

card: `console.log(x)` prints a value on its own line
`"Hi"` and `'Hi'` are strings, `42` is a number
End statements with `;`, comments start with `//`

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values with let and const and meet the basic types: number, string, boolean, undefined and null.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name for a value. You create one with `let`, a name, `=` and a value. After that, you use the name instead of the value. Names with several words are usually written in **camelCase**, like `firstName`.
A variable created with `let` can change. To give it a new value, write the name, `=` and the new value, without `let`. The old value is gone. The new value can use the old one.

Use `const` for a value that never changes. If you assign a new value to a `const`, the program stops with a `TypeError`. Many programmers use `const` by default and `let` only when the value must change.
Every value has a **type**. A `number` is any number, with or without a decimal point. A `string` is text. A `boolean` is either `true` or `false`.
Two special values mean that there is no value. `undefined` is the value of a variable that did not get a value yet. `null` is a value you set on purpose to say: empty.
The `typeof` operator gives you the type of a value, as a string.
`typeof null` gives `"object"`. This is an old mistake in JavaScript that can no longer be changed. Remember that `null` is a type of its own.

card: `let x = 5;` creates a variable you can change
`const y = 10;` creates a variable that cannot change
`typeof x` gives the type as a string, e.g. `"number"`

units.title: Operators and strings
units.summary: Calculate with numbers, compare values with === and !==, and build and change strings.

lesson.md: JavaScript has the usual **arithmetic operators**: `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. The operator `%` gives the remainder of a division, and `**` raises a number to a power: `2 ** 3` is `8`. `*` and `/` are calculated before `+` and `-`, like in math.
`x += 5` is a short form of `x = x + 5`. It also works with `-=`, `*=` and `/=`. `x++` adds `1` to `x`, and `x--` subtracts `1`.
`===` checks if two values are equal and gives `true` or `false`. `!==` checks if they are different. `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare sizes.
Always use `===` and `!==`. The older `==` changes the types before it compares, so `5 == "5"` is `true`. This causes bugs that are hard to find.
`+` joins strings. A **template literal** is often easier: write the string between backticks and put values inside `${...}`. JavaScript puts the value in place.

lesson.md: `length` is the number of characters in a string. `word[0]` is the first character, because positions start at `0`. Strings also have **methods**, which you call with a dot, like `toUpperCase()`. They return a new string and do not change the original.
`+` with a string and a number joins them as text. `"5" + 2` gives `"52"`, not `7`.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program choose with if and else, combine conditions with && and ||, and learn what truthy and falsy mean.

lesson.md: An `if` statement runs code only when a condition is `true`. Write the condition in parentheses and the code in curly braces `{ }`.
Add `else` for code that runs when the condition is `false`. With `else if`, you can check more conditions one after the other. Only the first block whose condition is `true` runs.

**Logical operators** combine conditions. `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are `true`. `||` (or) is `true` when at least one side is `true`. `!` (not) turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.
The **ternary operator** `condition ? a : b` is a short `if` and `else` that gives a value. The value is `a` if the condition is `true`, otherwise `b`.

A condition does not have to be a boolean. These values count as `false` and are called **falsy**: `false`, `0`, `""` (an empty string), `null`, `undefined` and `NaN` (not a number). All other values are **truthy**, even `"0"` and `"false"`. `Boolean(x)` shows you which one a value is.
Indent the code inside `{ }` by two spaces. JavaScript does not need it, but it makes your code much easier to read.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with for, while and for...of, and control loops with break and continue.

lesson.md: A **loop** repeats code. The `for` loop is the most common one. Its parentheses have three parts, separated by semicolons: a start (`let i = 1`), a condition (`i <= 3`) and a step (`i++`).

First, the loop runs the start. Then it checks the condition, runs the code in the braces and runs the step. It repeats this until the condition is `false`. A common pattern adds up values in a variable that you create before the loop.
A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. Use it when you do not know in advance how many times the loop must run.
Make sure that the condition becomes `false` at some point. If it never does, the loop runs forever and your program does not stop.
`for...of` goes through the items of a collection, one by one. With a string, you get each character. You will use it a lot in the world about arrays.
`break` stops the loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next round.

card: `for (const x of items) { ... }` goes through each item
`break` stops the loop, `continue` skips to the next round

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write reusable code with functions: parameters, return values, arrow functions and default parameters.

lesson.md: A **function** is a named block of code that you can run again and again. You define it with `function`, a name, parentheses and the code in curly braces. You run it by **calling** it: its name followed by `()`.
**Parameters** are names in the parentheses of the function. They get the values that you pass when you call the function. These values are called **arguments**.

lesson.output:
Good morning, Ada!
Good evening, Linus!

lesson.md: `return` sends a value back to the place where the function was called. The function stops at `return`. A function without `return` gives `undefined`.
`console.log` only shows a value. It does not give the value back. If you want to use the result of a function, use `return`.

An **arrow function** is a shorter way to write a function. You usually store it in a `const`. If the code is a single expression, you can leave out the curly braces and `return`. The value is then returned automatically.
A **default parameter** has a value that is used when the call leaves out the argument. Write it with `=` after the parameter name.

card: `const f = (x) => x * 2;` is an arrow function

units.title: Arrays
units.summary: Keep many values in one list: read and change items, add and remove them, and transform arrays with map and filter.

lesson.md: An **array** is an ordered list of values. You write it with square brackets `[ ]` and separate the items with commas. `console.log` shows the whole array, and `length` is the number of items.
Each item has an **index**, its position. The first item has index `0`, the second has index `1`, and so on. The last item has index `length - 1`. You can also change an item through its index.
You can change the items of an array in a `const`. `const` only means that the variable always holds the same array.
`push()` adds an item at the end. `pop()` removes the last item and returns it. `includes()` checks if an item is in the array.
`for...of` gives you each item. The method `forEach()` does the same with a function: it calls the function once for every item.

`map()` creates a **new** array: it calls a function for every item and keeps the results. `filter()` creates a new array with only the items for which the function returns `true`. The original array does not change.

card: `const a = [1, 2, 3];` and `a[0]` is the first item
`a.forEach((x) => console.log(x))` runs code for each item

units.title: Objects
units.summary: Group related data in objects: read and change properties, write methods, use destructuring and turn objects into JSON.

lesson.md: An **object** groups values that belong together. Each value has a name, called a **key**. Together they form a **property**. You write an object with curly braces and `key: value` pairs, separated by commas.
You read and change a property with a dot, like `user.age`. You add a new property in the same way. A property that does not exist gives `undefined`.
With square brackets, you write the key as a string: `user["name"]`. This is useful when the key is stored in a variable.
A function inside an object is called a **method**. Inside a method, `this` is the object itself, so the method can use the other properties.
**Destructuring** takes properties out of an object and stores them in variables with the same names, all in one line.
`JSON.stringify()` turns an object into a string in the **JSON** format. Programs often use JSON to send data to each other, for example over the internet.

lesson.code:
const point = { x: 3, y: 4, label: "A" };
console.log(JSON.stringify(point));
